title: Agent loops: termination, budgets, compounding error
story:
An agent is a model running inside a loop with access to tools. It observes, decides on a next step, calls something outside itself — a query, a command, a calculation, a request — inspects the result, and repeats until it judges the goal met. That last clause is where all the difficulty lives: the loop's termination condition is produced by the same component whose reliability is in question.

The arithmetic of the loop is the thing to internalise, because it is not intuitive and it is not empirical — it follows from multiplication alone.

Suppose each step succeeds independently with some probability. Then the probability the whole chain succeeds is that number raised to the number of steps. Take a step reliability of nine in ten, which sounds respectable. Over five steps the chain succeeds a little under six times in ten. Over ten steps, a little over a third. Nothing has degraded and no error has compounded in any mysterious way; the same multiplication has simply been applied twice as often.

Read the implication in the other direction, because it is the useful one. To get a ten-step chain to succeed nine times in ten, each step has to succeed about ninety-nine times in a hundred. Small improvements in per-step reliability produce large improvements in chain reliability, and a chain long enough will defeat any per-step reliability you can actually reach. So the first design question about an agent is not how good the model is. It is how many steps you have allowed it.

Which means the shortest correct chain is worth more than a better model, and this is where most of the available engineering actually is. Every step removed from the loop multiplies through. Replacing three tool calls with one deterministic function does more for the success rate than any prompt.

The second failure has nothing to do with the arithmetic and is the one that produces bills. When a tool returns something the agent did not expect, the natural next action is to try again — and the agent's judgement about whether to try again is produced by the same faculty that just misjudged the call. So it retries with a slight variation, gets a similar error, and retries again. Nothing in the loop is watching the loop, and the retry costs money every time.

Notice that this is not an unlikely edge case. It is the default behaviour of a loop whose exit condition is generated from inside it, and the standard local fix — an instruction to give up after a few tries — is evaluated by the same component. The counter has to live outside.

So the engineering is defensive and mostly unglamorous. A hard limit on steps, enforced by the loop rather than requested of the model. A hard limit on spend, enforced the same way. Validation of tool arguments against a schema before the call happens, so a malformed call fails immediately and cheaply rather than producing an error the agent will try to reason about. A distinct path for a human when the budget is exhausted, because the alternative to escalating is failing silently.

One limit worth stating, since the arithmetic can be read too pessimistically. Independence is an assumption, and a real chain is not independent: a step that verifies the previous step's work, or a tool that fails loudly rather than returning something plausible, breaks the multiplication in your favour. That is the actual argument for verification steps — not that checking is virtuous, but that a checked step changes the exponent's base. The pessimistic calculation describes an unverified chain, which is precisely the design worth arguing against.

problem.name: The loop's exponent
problem.shape: A model decides its own next action in a loop, and also decides when to stop.
tell: the number of steps is unbounded or set by the model
spend is discovered after the fact rather than capped before
a failing tool call is retried with rephrased arguments
the success rate is discussed per step and not per task
problem.move: Count the steps first and shorten the chain before improving anything else, because every step removed multiplies through. Then put the limits outside the loop: a step count and a spend cap enforced by the caller, argument validation before each call, and an explicit human path when a budget runs out.
problem.invariant: If steps succeed independently, task success is per-step reliability raised to the number of steps — so chain length and per-step reliability trade against each other exponentially, and any fixed reliability is defeated by a long enough chain.
problem.breaks: Independence is an assumption, not a property. A step that verifies the previous one, or a tool that fails loudly rather than returning something plausible, breaks the multiplication favourably — which is the real argument for verification steps, since they change the base rather than merely adding caution. The pessimistic figure describes an unverified chain.

cost.time: validation before every call, and chains deliberately kept short, which limits what a single invocation can accomplish
cost.space: budget and step state held outside the loop, plus a schema per tool
cost.beats: trusting the model to stop, which is evaluated by the faculty whose judgement is in question, and running without limits, which works until a tool returns something unexpected

problem.practice: Take an agent task you have and count the tool calls in a successful run. Raise your honest per-step reliability to that power, then compare the result to what you tell people the success rate is.

beats.broke: A loop decides its own next action and its own stopping point, so the component whose reliability is in question is also the one judging whether to continue — and nothing outside is counting.
beats.fix: Count the steps first and shorten the chain, since every step removed multiplies through, then enforce step and spend limits from outside the loop rather than requesting them of the model.
beats.cost: Short chains limit what one invocation can achieve, and validation runs before every call — while the arithmetic itself only holds for an unverified chain, so it must not be quoted as a law.
